agree.reason: The note is candid and gives concrete support: the partners will also be in three days, there is a commuting stipend, desks are coming, and the policy will be reviewed. Most staff will go along, but a remote hire who lives 1–2 hours away gets no accommodation beyond the stipend and may still leave.

honest.reason: The facts match what the writer had, and the link between the junior delays and remote work is hedged properly ('we think that's part of the gap'). One line overreaches: 'we lost it because of how we came across' states as cause what the clients only gave as feedback.

works_the_facts.reason: The figures are repeated as given and never developed: the 30% delay isn't turned into months, the 15 remote hires aren't shown as a third of the 46 staff, and nothing says what the hospital losses cost or what continuing as now would mean.

right_comparison.reason: The current setup is implied by the lost bids and the slower development of juniors, and the partners' own one-day pattern is set against the new rule. But the note never says outright what happens if nothing changes, and it gives no trend.

qualification.reason: The six-month review has a rough date. It has no measure, such as interview wins or how fast juniors reach project lead, and no stated consequence if the policy isn't working, so readers have nothing they can check.

objections.reason: The note faces the main objection directly ('a real change to the job you took on') and covers the obvious practical concerns: desks, commuting cost, and whether the partners will also come in. It doesn't explain why three days rather than fewer, and it offers nothing to remote hires who live under two hours away but still far.

fit.reason: It is a one-page email with a clear subject line and short, headed sections, and it leads into the Friday meeting as the brief asked.
